Embryonated eggs of European sea sturgeon Acipenser sturio, incubated at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], complete their development and hatch after approximately 3 days , a duration that aligns with the extended incubation periods documented for large-bodied acipenserids. The newly emerged prolarvae measure roughly 0.93 cm  in total length, a modest size that reflects the considerable yolk reserves still available to the endotrophic larva. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva remains in a lecithotrophic state for a relatively brief period. At a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the onset of exogenous feeding begins after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days] as the yolk is largely consumed and the mouth gape becomes functional. This rapid transition from endogenous to exogenous nutrition is an important developmental milestone, and the shift is marked by the emergence of a small but active free-swimming individual. At the moment of birth, when the larva emerges from the chorion and begins its free-living existence, the total length of the young is about 1.5 cm [Lb = about 1.5 cm].

The juvenile period in Acipenser sturio encompasses a prolonged phase of somatic growth and habitat transition. Metamorphosis, the developmental process transforming the larval body plan into the juvenile morphology, occurs when individuals reach a total length of approximately 4.5 cm , a size that is attained after roughly 63 days  when larvae are reared at a stable temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. At this stage, the young fish begin to resemble miniature adults, displaying the characteristic scute rows and elongated snout of the species. This transition marks the onset of a more benthic lifestyle, as the juveniles begin foraging on the riverbed for insect larvae and small crustaceans. The duration of the larval phase is relatively short compared to the extended juvenile stage that follows, which can last for several years as individuals grow slowly in freshwater habitats before beginning their catadromous migration toward estuarine and marine environments. Sexual maturation is reached at approximately 10 years after hatching [tp = 10 years after hatching], a value consistent with the general pattern observed in other members of the genus Acipenser, though the precise timing may vary with local thermal conditions.

As individuals approach sexual maturation, body size becomes an increasingly important determinant of reproductive potential. The total length at puberty, the point at which gonadal development commences and individuals become capable of reproducing, has been recorded at approximately 150 cm [Lp = approximately 150 cm] in both sexes. This substantial size threshold reflects the considerable energetic investment required for migration, gamete production, and spawning behavior. Females in particular attain puberty later than males, with first reproduction documented at 14 years after hatching [tR = 14 years after hatching] when maintained under the thermal regime typical of their native rivers (20 °C [T = 20 °C]). This delayed maturation is a common life-history strategy among large, long-lived sturgeon species and is linked to the necessity of reaching a critical body size that can support the considerable metabolic costs of reproduction. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is triggered by a combination of photoperiodic cues and accumulated energy reserves, ensuring that spawning occurs only when conditions are favorable for offspring survival. Field surveys suggest that first spawning typically occurs during the spring flood pulse, when river temperatures begin to rise.

The maximum body size attained by European sea sturgeon is truly remarkable among freshwater and anadromous fishes. The ultimate total length, representing the asymptotic size achieved by the largest individuals in the population, reaches up to 500 cm [Li = up to 500 cm] in the wild. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of these exceptionally large adults has been estimated at approximately 460,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 460,000 grams], a figure derived from allometric scaling relationships observed in related sturgeon species. This immense body mass is supported by a robust skeletal structure and extensive lipid reserves that fuel the long-distance migrations characteristic of the species. The maximum lifespan in the species has been estimated at approximately 120 years [am = approximately 120 years], a value that underscores the extremely slow life-history pace of this l at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]ong-lived fish. At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], which represents the average thermal condition experienced by adults during their non-migratory periods, individuals exhibit exceptionally low metabolic rates that contribute to their extended longevity. These life-history traits place Acipenser sturio among the most long-lived and slow-maturing vertebrates in European freshwater systems.

Reproductive output in Acipenser sturio is characterized by high fecundity, a strategy typical of many long-lived, iteroparous fish species that experience high early-life mortality. Adult females are capable of producing large numbers of eggs per spawning event, with the maximum reproductive rate reported as 1,500 eggs per day [Ri = 1,500 eggs per day] under the optimal thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This remarkable daily egg production is sustained by the large body size and extensive ovarian development of mature females, which can carry millions of oocytes prior to spawning. The spawning migration itself is a energetically demanding journey upriver, often exceeding hundreds of kilometers, and is timed to coincide with specific temperature and flow conditions that favor egg survival and larval development. After spawning, adults typically return to estuarine or marine feeding grounds to replenish their energy reserves before the next reproductive cycle. The combination of delayed maturity, high fecundity, and iteroparity represents a classic bet-hedging life-history strategy that buffers the population against the high variability in recruitment success that characterizes anadromous fish in dynamic riverine environments. Long-term monitoring programs have documented significant interannual variation in spawning success, linked primarily to hydrological conditions.
